query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The persistence of corrosion resistance in pre‐exposed Q235 steel is governed by the integrity and composition of its native oxide layer. A well-developed, adherent Fe3O4-rich film formed during initial exposure serves as a barrier against aggressive salt attack at both room temperature and high temperatures (700–900 °C), whereas its absence or degradation promotes accelerated corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre‐exposure state with an intact native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Mechanically remove or inhibit the formation of the native oxide layer on some Q235 specimens, while leaving a control group with the oxide intact.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets of specimens to aggressive salt environments under room temperature and high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C). The hypothesis applies under conditions where salt is aggressive enough to attack the metal surface, and it should not apply when alternative corrosion inhibitors or protective coatings are present.
generation.structural_mediator: The thickness, continuity, and phase composition (primarily Fe3O4 content) of the native oxide film.
generation.mechanism: An intact native oxide film (Fe3O4-rich) acts as a physical and chemical barrier that reduces ion transport and corrosion reactions. When this barrier is compromised or absent, corrosive species can more easily penetrate the metal substrate, accelerating degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens with the intact native oxide film will show lower mass loss, less pit formation, and overall reduced surface degradation compared to specimens from which the protective oxide layer has been removed. This effect should be observed under both room-temperature and high-temperature salt exposures.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel with its natural, pre‐exposure oxide layer in a controlled salt environment, serving as a reference for corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism and observed protection will primarily manifest under aggressive salt exposures; in milder conditions or with additional protective treatments (e.g., coatings), the role of the native oxide may be less significant.
generation.uncertainty: The exact protective contribution of the native oxide layer may vary depending on its microstructural heterogeneity and the specific salt chemistry. The relative importance of thermal effects at high temperatures compared to room temperature also remains to be fully delineated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel specimens. For Set A, retain the native oxide film; for Set B, remove the native oxide film via careful surface polishing followed by minimal subsequent oxidation. Expose both sets to identical aggressive salt environments at room temperature and at 700–900 °C for a fixed duration. Characterize the oxide film structure and composition pre-exposure (via XRD, SEM-EDS) and quantify corrosion degradation post-exposure (via mass loss measurements, surface profilometry, and microscopy).
measurements: Thickness and composition of the oxide layer (pre- and post-exposure) using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Surface roughness and pit density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of the native oxide layer does not result in significantly worsened corrosion (i.e., mass loss, pit formation, and degradation comparable to specimens with the intact oxide) under both temperature regimes, then the hypothesis that the native oxide layer is the primary mediator of corrosion protection in Q235 steel will be falsified.
